cards.q: For the image matrix shown below, the value of M is ___, the value of N is ___, and the pixel value at the origin is ___.
cards.ans: M = 4, N = 3, and the pixel value at the origin is 101.
cards.varies: Only one attempt was captured, so this is not confirmed. Expect a different matrix size and different values in the test.
method: Count the rows going down. That number is M.
Count the columns going across. That number is N.
The origin is coordinate (1,1), the top-left entry. Read that value.
cards.check: M × N must equal the number of entries in the matrix. Here 4 × 3 = 12 entries.
cards.trap: Swapping M and N. M is rows and comes first. A tall, narrow matrix has M larger than N.

cards.q: In image processing, we use the (i,j) coordinate system. Given the image matrix below, what is the value of the pixel at coordinate (3,4)?
cards.varies: Only one attempt was captured, so this is not confirmed. Expect a different coordinate or matrix in the test.
method: Read (i,j) as row i, then column j. Count from 1 at the top-left.
Go down to row i.
Go across that row to entry j. Read the value.
cards.check: Read the swapped coordinate (j,i) as well. If it gives a different value, make sure you entered the (i,j) one.
cards.trap: Reading (3,4) as (x,y), which means column 3, row 4. That gives 5 here, and the right answer is 1.

cards.q: Match the images to their image formats.
cards.ans: A is greyscale. B is indexed. C is vector. D is RGB. E is binary.
cards.varies: The five pictures look fixed. Canvas may change the order of the rows.
method: Find the picture with only pure black and pure white. That is binary. Find the wire mesh of triangles. That is vector, because a vector image is made of points and lines.
Find the picture with smooth greys and no colour. That is greyscale.
Two colour pictures are left. Look at the background. Flat bands of colour mean indexed, because an indexed image has few colours. A smooth fade means RGB.
cards.check: Each format is used once. If one format is used twice, one of the two colour pictures is wrong.
cards.trap: Mixing up indexed and RGB. Both are colour. The banded background is the sign of indexed.

cards.q: What is the total number of pixels in an image with 3 rows and 20 columns that has 4 colour channels?
cards.varies: The number of rows, the number of columns and the number of colour channels.
method: Multiply rows by columns. Pixels = M × N.
Ignore the number of colour channels. Channels add values to each pixel. They do not add pixels.
cards.check: The answer must be M × N exactly, with no other number in it.
cards.trap: Multiplying by the channel count. 3 × 20 × 4 = 240 is wrong.

working: Each pixel holds 4 values, but it is still one pixel.

cards.q: How many bytes of memory are needed to store an image with 323 rows and 429 columns in binary format? (note: consider pixel values only, ignoring any possible header/footer information). Formula: S_binary = ⌈MN ÷ 8⌉
cards.varies: The number of rows and the number of columns.
method: A binary pixel needs 1 bit. Work out MN to get the number of bits.
Divide by 8 to change bits to bytes.
If the result is not a whole number, round it up to the next whole number. The ⌈ ⌉ brackets mean round up.
cards.check: Multiply the answer by 8. It must be equal to MN or up to 7 more than MN.
cards.trap: Rounding to the nearest whole number. A part of a byte still needs a whole byte, so 17,320.125 would also become 17,321.

cards.q: How many bytes of memory are needed to store an image with 605 rows and 348 columns that contains 87 unique shades of grey in 8-bit greyscale format? (note: consider pixel values only, ignoring any possible header/footer information). Formula: S_greyscale = MN
cards.varies: The number of rows, the number of columns and the number of unique shades of grey.
method: An 8-bit greyscale pixel needs 1 byte. Bytes = M × N.
Ignore the number of unique shades. Every pixel takes 1 byte, whatever its value.
cards.check: The answer is 8 times the binary size for the same M and N.
cards.trap: Using the 87 shades in the sum. The number of shades is extra information that the formula does not use.

cards.q: How many bytes of memory are needed to store an RGB image with 210 rows and 145 columns that has 13 unique colours in RGB colour format? (note: consider pixel values only, ignoring any other possible header/footer information). Formula: S_rgb = 3MN
cards.varies: The number of rows, the number of columns and the number of unique colours.
method: An RGB pixel needs 3 bytes, one each for red, green and blue. Bytes = 3 × M × N.
Ignore the number of unique colours. RGB format has no colour table.
cards.check: The answer divides exactly by 3, and answer ÷ 3 = MN.
cards.trap: Using the indexed formula MN + 3C because the question gives a colour count. The format named in the question decides the formula. Here it says RGB colour format.

cards.q: How many bytes of memory are needed to store an image with 248 colours that has 504 rows and 312 columns in indexed colour format? (note: consider pixel values and the CLUT only, ignoring any other possible header/footer information). Formula: S_indexed = MN + 3C
cards.varies: The number of colours, the number of rows and the number of columns.
method: Each pixel stores one index, which takes 1 byte. That part is M × N.
The colour look-up table (CLUT) stores C colours at 3 bytes each. That part is 3 × C.
Add the two parts.
cards.check: The answer is a little more than MN and much less than 3MN.
cards.trap: Leaving out the table, or multiplying MN by 3. Only the table entries take 3 bytes each. This is the one format where the colour count matters.

cards.q: How many different shades of grey are possible (v) in a greyscale image that uses 17 bits-per-pixel (t)? Formula: v = 2^t
method: Each extra bit doubles the number of shades. Work out 2 to the power t.
cards.check: The answer is an even number. 2¹⁰ = 1,024 is a useful anchor: 2¹⁷ = 1,024 × 128.
cards.trap: Subtracting 1. The number of shades is 2^t. The largest value is 2^t − 1.

cards.q: What is the maximum possible pixel value (v_max) in a greyscale image that uses 24 bits-per-pixel (t)? Formula: v_max = 2^t − 1
method: Work out 2 to the power t, as in card 9.
Subtract 1, because pixel values start at 0.
cards.check: The answer is an odd number. For t = 8 the same rule gives 255.
cards.trap: Giving 2^t. That is the number of shades, which is one more than the largest value.

cards.q: What is the minimum number of bits-per-pixel (t) that would be needed to store a greyscale medical image of size 530 × 716 pixels that needs to be able to represent up to 20825 shades of grey (v)? Formula: t = ⌈log₂(v)⌉, such that log₂(x) = log_a(x) ÷ log_a(2), e.g., log₂(x) = log₁₀(x) ÷ log₁₀(2) = ln(x) ÷ ln(2)
cards.varies: The image size and the number of shades of grey, v.
method: Ignore the image size. Only the number of shades v matters.
On the calculator, work out log(v) ÷ log(2).
Round the result up to the next whole number.
cards.check: 2^t must be at least v, and 2^(t−1) must be less than v. Here 2¹⁵ = 32,768 is enough and 2¹⁴ = 16,384 is not.
cards.trap: Rounding 14.35 to the nearest whole number, which gives 14. With 14 bits there are only 16,384 shades. Always round up.

cards.q: How many different binary images of size 7 × 3 pixels are possible? Formula: kⁿ
method: k is the number of values one pixel can take. For binary, k = 2.
n is the number of pixels. n = M × N.
Work out k to the power n.
cards.check: The answer is a power of 2. Halve it n times and you reach 1.
cards.trap: Using M or N alone as the power, or multiplying k by n. The power is the full pixel count M × N.

cards.q: How many different 8-bit greyscale images of size 2 × 2 pixels are possible? Formula: kⁿ
method: Same method as card 12. The only change is k.
An 8-bit pixel can take 2⁸ = 256 values, so k = 256.
cards.check: 256⁴ = 2³². Type the full number with no rounding. A calculator that shows 4.294967296 × 10⁹ still gives every digit.
cards.trap: Using k = 8 or k = 255. An 8-bit pixel has 256 possible values, 0 to 255.

cards.q: How many different RGB images of size 1 × 1 pixel are possible?
cards.varies: Only one attempt was captured, so this is not confirmed. The question type is Numeric, not Formula, so the size may stay 1 × 1.
method: Same method as card 12. The only change is k.
An RGB pixel has three 8-bit channels. Each channel has 256 values, so k = 256 × 256 × 256 = 16,777,216.
A 1 × 1 image has n = 1, so the answer is k itself.
cards.check: The answer is 2²⁴, which is one more than the largest 24-bit value in card 10.
cards.trap: Answering 256 or 3 × 256 = 768. The three channels multiply, because every red value can go with every green value and every blue value.

cards.q: The RGB colourspace mixes the red, green and blue primary colours of light in different proportions to produce a range of other colours (called the gamut of the colourspace). It is usually represented as cubic coordinate system. Match the RGB triplets to the corresponding colours.
cards.varies: The nine triplets look fixed. Canvas may change the order of the rows.
method: The triplet order is (red, green, blue). One channel at 255 and the others at 0 gives that primary colour.
Two channels at 255 give a secondary colour. Red + green is yellow. Green + blue is cyan. Red + blue is magenta.
Three equal channels give a grey. All 0 is black, all 255 is white, and all 128 is mid grey.
cards.check: Each secondary colour is missing one channel. Yellow has no blue. Cyan has no red. Magenta has no green.
cards.trap: Thinking of paint. In light, red + green makes yellow. Red + blue makes magenta, not purple or yellow.
